subject: IB Diploma Chemistry
name: IB Chemistry
about: IB Diploma Chemistry teaching-hour plan. Hours from the IB guide; lesson durations share each topic's hours. Built by lessongen/ib_plan.py.
source: IB Chemistry guide, first assessment 2025: recommended teaching hours per topic (syllabus content SL 110 h, HL 180 h; experimental programme SL 40 h, HL 60 h)..

themes.S1: Models of the particulate nature of matter
themes.R2: How much, how fast and how far?
themes.R3: What are the mechanisms of chemical change?

topics.name: Introduction to the particulate nature of matter

lessons.title: Elements, compounds and mixtures, and how the properties of the components let us separate a mixture
The kinetic molecular theory, changes of state and heating curves, and the Kelvin scale as a measure of average kinetic energy
The nuclear model of the atom: protons, neutrons and electrons, their relative masses and charges, and nuclear symbols
Isotopes: same element, different numbers of neutrons, their properties, and relative atomic mass from isotopic abundance
Mass spectra of elements: how a mass spectrometer works and how to read isotopic composition and relative atomic mass from a spectrum
Emission spectra: continuous and line spectra, the electromagnetic spectrum, and how the hydrogen spectrum shows discrete energy levels
Main energy levels (2n² electrons), sublevels s, p, d and f, atomic orbitals and the shapes of s and p orbitals
Writing full and condensed electron configurations and orbital diagrams up to Z = 36 using the Aufbau principle, Hund's rule and the Pauli principle
The convergence limit of the hydrogen emission spectrum and calculating the first ionization energy from it
Successive ionization energies as evidence for main energy levels and sublevels, and deducing the group of an element

topics.name: Counting particles by mass: The mole

lessons.title: The mole as the SI unit of amount of substance, the Avogadro constant, and converting between amount and number of particles
Relative atomic mass and relative formula mass on the carbon-12 scale, including hydrated salts
Molar mass in g mol⁻¹ and the triangle n = m ÷ M linking mass, amount and number of particles
Empirical and molecular formulas from masses, percentage composition and combustion data
Molar concentration, mass concentration, standard solutions and dilution
Avogadro's law: equal volumes of gases contain equal numbers of particles, and volume ratios in reactions of gases
The ideal gas model and why real gases deviate from it at low temperature and high pressure
The molar volume of an ideal gas at STP and calculations linking gas volume, amount and mass
The ideal gas equation pV = nRT, the gas laws and their graphs, and finding molar mass experimentally
Forming cations and anions: predicting ionic charges from the periodic table, and transition elements with more than one ion
The ionic bond as electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions, and writing and naming formulas including polyatomic ions
Ionic lattices, lattice enthalpy and how the ionic model explains the properties of ionic compounds
The covalent bond as the attraction between a shared pair of electrons and two nuclei, the octet rule and drawing Lewis formulas
Single, double and triple bonds, the link between bond order, length and strength, and coordination (dative) bonds
VSEPR theory: electron domains, electron domain geometry and molecular geometry for two, three and four domains
Electronegativity, bond polarity and partial charges
Molecular polarity: how bond polarity and molecular geometry together decide whether a molecule has a net dipole
Covalent network structures of carbon (diamond, graphite, graphene, fullerene) and silicon and silicon dioxide, and their properties
Intermolecular forces: London dispersion forces, dipole–induced dipole, dipole–dipole forces and hydrogen bonding
Relative strengths of intermolecular forces and how they explain volatility, boiling points, solubility and conductivity of molecular substances
Chromatography: separation by relative attraction to the mobile and stationary phases, paper and thin-layer chromatography, and Rf values
Resonance structures, delocalized electrons and fractional bond orders in ozone, carbonate, nitrate and carboxylate ions
Benzene: evidence against the Kekulé structure and the delocalized π electron ring
Expanded octets and the shapes of molecules with five and six electron domains
Formal charge and using it to choose the preferred Lewis formula
Sigma and pi bonds: head-on and sideways overlap of orbitals, and counting σ and π bonds in molecules
Hybridization: sp³, sp² and sp hybrid orbitals and linking them to electron domains and molecular shape
Metallic bonding as a lattice of cations in a sea of delocalized electrons, and how it explains conductivity, malleability and ductility
The strength of metallic bonding: how ionic charge and radius explain melting point trends across period 3 and down group 1
Transition elements and their delocalized d-electrons: high melting points, conductivity and strength
Bonding as a continuum between ionic, covalent and metallic models, and using the bonding (van Arkel–Ketelaar) triangle
Alloys as mixtures of a metal with other metals or non-metals, and why their properties are enhanced
Polymers as macromolecules of repeating units, addition polymerization of alkenes, and the properties and environmental impact of plastics
Condensation polymers: polyesters and polyamides, the small molecule released, and their hydrolysis and biodegradability

topics.name: The periodic table: Classification of elements

lessons.title: Periods, groups and blocks of the periodic table, and linking an element's position to its electron configuration
Periodic trends in atomic radius and ionic radius explained by nuclear charge, shielding and energy levels
Periodic trends in first ionization energy, electron affinity and electronegativity
Group trends: the reactivity of group 1 metals with water and of group 17 halogens in displacement reactions
The metallic to non-metallic continuum and the acid–base character of the oxides of period 3
Oxidation states: the rules for assigning them, and naming compounds and oxyanions with Roman numerals
Discontinuities in first ionization energy across a period: the dips at group 13 and group 16 as evidence for sublevels and electron pairing
Transition elements: incomplete d sublevels and their characteristic properties (variable oxidation states, complex ions, colour, catalysis, magnetism)
Variable oxidation states of transition elements: why they occur and the common oxidation states of the first row
Why transition element complexes are coloured: splitting of d orbitals by ligands, absorption of light and complementary colours

topics.name: Functional groups: Classification of organic compounds

lessons.title: Representing organic molecules: empirical, molecular, full and condensed structural, skeletal and stereochemical formulas
Functional groups and the classes of organic compounds they define
Homologous series, their general formulas, and trends in physical properties such as boiling point and solubility
IUPAC naming I: alkanes, alkenes, alkynes and halogenoalkanes, including branched chains and locants
IUPAC naming II: alcohols, aldehydes, ketones, carboxylic acids, ethers, esters, amines and amides
Structural isomers: chain, position and functional group isomers
Classifying alcohols, halogenoalkanes and amines as primary, secondary or tertiary, and isomer practice
Stereoisomers I: conformational and configurational isomers, and cis–trans isomerism in alkenes and cycloalkanes
Stereoisomers II: chiral carbons, enantiomers, optical activity, polarimetry and racemic mixtures
Mass spectrometry of organic compounds: the molecular ion and fragmentation patterns
Infrared spectroscopy: bond vibrations, absorption ranges and identifying functional groups
¹H NMR spectroscopy I: hydrogen environments, number of signals, chemical shift and the TMS reference
¹H NMR spectroscopy II: integration traces, relative numbers of hydrogens and assigning spectra
¹H NMR spectroscopy III: spin–spin splitting and the n + 1 rule (singlets, doublets, triplets, quartets)
Combined structural analysis I: index of hydrogen deficiency and combining MS and IR data
Combined structural analysis II: solving full problems with MS, IR and ¹H NMR together
Energy transfer between a system and its surroundings, conservation of energy, and the difference between heat and temperature
Exothermic and endothermic reactions, the sign of ΔH, relative stability, and energy profile diagrams
Standard enthalpy change ΔH⦵, calculating heat transferred with Q = mcΔT, and enthalpy changes of reactions in solution
Calorimetry experiments: measuring enthalpy of combustion and of reactions in solution, temperature–time graphs, and sources of error
Bond breaking and bond forming, average bond enthalpies, and estimating ΔH from bond enthalpy data
Hess's law and constructing energy cycles to find enthalpy changes that cannot be measured directly
Hess's law by combining thermochemical equations: reversing, multiplying and adding
Standard enthalpy changes of formation and combustion: definitions, equations and data
Calculating ΔH from enthalpy of formation data and from enthalpy of combustion data
Born–Haber cycles: the enthalpy steps in forming an ionic solid and calculating lattice enthalpy
Born–Haber cycles in practice: unknown steps, comparing lattice enthalpies and explaining which ionic compounds form
Complete and incomplete combustion of metals, non-metals and organic compounds, and the hazards of carbon monoxide and soot
Fossil fuels: coal, crude oil and natural gas, their specific energy and energy density, and their advantages and disadvantages
Biofuels: carbon fixed recently by photosynthesis, bioethanol, biodiesel and biogas, and whether they are carbon neutral
Fuel cells: converting chemical energy directly to electrical energy, the hydrogen and methanol fuel cells, and their advantages
Entropy as a measure of dispersal of matter and energy, predicting the sign of ΔS, and calculating standard entropy changes
Gibbs energy change, ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, and calculating ΔG⦵ with consistent units
Spontaneity: the sign of ΔG, the four combinations of ΔH and ΔS, and the temperature at which a reaction becomes spontaneous
Gibbs energy and equilibrium: why ΔG becomes less negative as a reaction proceeds and reaches zero at equilibrium

topics.name: How much? The amount of chemical change

lessons.title: Balanced chemical equations with state symbols, and ionic equations with spectator ions
Reacting masses: using mole ratios to calculate the masses of reactants and products
Mole ratios with gas volumes and solution concentrations, including titration calculations
The limiting reactant, reactants in excess, and the theoretical yield
Percentage yield: comparing experimental and theoretical yield, and why yields are below 100 %
Atom economy as a measure of efficiency in green chemistry, and comparing synthetic routes

topics.name: How fast? The rate of chemical change

lessons.title: Rate of reaction as change in concentration per unit time, its units, and finding rates from the gradients of graphs
Experimental methods for measuring rate: gas volume, mass loss, colour change, conductivity and clock reactions
Collision theory: particles must collide with sufficient energy and correct orientation
How concentration, pressure, surface area and temperature affect rate, explained by collision theory
Activation energy and the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution: explaining the effect of temperature on the fraction of particles able to react
Catalysts: providing an alternative pathway with lower activation energy, shown on energy profiles and Maxwell–Boltzmann curves
Investigating rate in practice: designing, carrying out and evaluating a rate experiment
Reaction mechanisms: elementary steps, intermediates, the rate-determining step and energy profiles of multi-step reactions
Molecularity of elementary steps, and why rate equations must be found experimentally and can be linked to mechanisms
Orders of reaction: deducing orders from initial-rate data and from concentration–time and rate–concentration graphs
The rate constant k: calculating it from data, deducing its units from the overall order, and its temperature dependence
The Arrhenius equation: finding activation energy from ln k against 1/T, and the meaning of the frequency factor A

topics.name: How far? The extent of chemical change

lessons.title: Dynamic equilibrium in a closed system: equal forward and backward rates and constant concentrations
The equilibrium law: writing equilibrium constant expressions (K) for homogeneous equilibria
The magnitude of K and the extent of reaction at equilibrium
Le Châtelier's principle: effects of concentration, pressure, temperature and catalysts on position of equilibrium and on K, with industrial examples
The reaction quotient Q and comparing it with K to predict the direction a reaction will shift
Quantifying equilibrium composition: ICE tables, calculating K from initial and equilibrium data, and equilibrium concentrations from K
Linking equilibrium and thermodynamics: ΔG⦵ = −RT ln K, and calculating K from ΔG⦵ and vice versa
Brønsted–Lowry acids and bases: proton donors and acceptors, and conjugate acid–base pairs
Amphiprotic species, and neutralization reactions of acids with bases, carbonates and metals
The pH scale: pH = −log₁₀[H⁺], calculating pH and [H⁺], and measuring pH
The ionic product of water, Kw, and the pH of strong bases
Strong and weak acids and bases: extent of ionization, and experiments that distinguish them
Acid–base titrations and pH curves for strong acid–strong base reactions
pOH, pKw and the relationship pH + pOH = 14 at 298 K; temperature dependence of Kw
Acid and base dissociation constants Ka, Kb, pKa and pKb, and calculating the pH of weak acids and bases
Conjugate pairs: Ka × Kb = Kw and pKa + pKb = pKw, and the inverse strengths of conjugates
The pH of salt solutions: hydrolysis of ions from weak acids and weak bases
pH curves involving weak acids and weak bases: shape, buffer region, half-equivalence (pH = pKa) and equivalence pH
Acid–base indicators as weak acids, their pH range, and choosing the right indicator for a titration
Buffer solutions: composition, how they resist pH change, and calculating buffer pH
Oxidation and reduction: electron transfer, oxidation states, oxygen and hydrogen, and oxidizing and reducing agents
Half-equations, and balancing redox equations in acidic solution
Relative ease of oxidation and reduction: the activity series of metals and halogens, displacement reactions, and acids with metals
Primary (voltaic) cells: converting chemical energy from spontaneous redox reactions into electrical energy
Secondary (rechargeable) cells and fuel cells: advantages, disadvantages and the redox reactions involved
Electrolytic cells: using electrical energy to drive non-spontaneous redox, and electrolysis of molten salts
Oxidation of organic compounds: primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols with acidified dichromate
Reduction of organic compounds: carboxylic acids, aldehydes and ketones to alcohols, and hydrogenation of alkenes and alkynes
Standard electrode potentials and the standard hydrogen electrode
Standard cell potentials, predicting spontaneity, and the link ΔG⦵ = −nFE⦵
Electrolysis of aqueous solutions: competing reactions of water and the effects of electrode and concentration
Electroplating: coating objects with a metal film, and quantitative aspects
Radicals: species with unpaired electrons, formed by homolytic fission using UV light or heat
Radical substitution of alkanes: initiation, propagation and termination, and why a mixture of products forms
Nucleophiles as electron-pair donors, and heterolytic fission forming ions
Nucleophilic substitution of halogenoalkanes with hydroxide ions to form alcohols
Electrophiles as electron-pair acceptors, and the electron-rich C=C bond
Electrophilic addition reactions of alkenes with hydrogen halides, halogens and water
Lewis acids and bases: electron-pair acceptors and donors, and nucleophiles and electrophiles as Lewis bases and acids
Coordination bonds in complex ions: ligands as Lewis bases, coordination number and formulas of complexes
Mechanisms of nucleophilic substitution: SN1 and SN2, rate equations and stereochemistry
Factors affecting the rate of nucleophilic substitution: the leaving group, the class of halogenoalkane, the nucleophile and the solvent
Mechanism of electrophilic addition with carbocations, and Markovnikov's rule for asymmetric alkenes
Electrophilic substitution of benzene: nitration mechanism and why benzene substitutes rather than adds
